head: Most men|don't collapse.|They *erode*.
body: Chapter 2 — The Slow Death of Drifters

Nobody wakes up and says "I want to drift."

Nobody writes a five-year plan for becoming soft, distracted, financially exposed and easy to control.

That's exactly *why it works*.

head: Drift comes|dressed like|normal life.
body:
"I just need a little more time."
"Once I get this one thing handled, I'm locking in."

Those sentences don't sound fatal.
That's *the whole point*.

A man without direction doesn't become neutral.

He becomes *available*.

Available to distraction. To appetite. To fear. To other people's agendas. To whatever is loudest in the room that week.

If you aren't directing your life, *something weaker will*.

And weaker things are always hiring.

Comfort will hire you. Lust will hire you. Entertainment will hire you. Excuses will hire you. Fear will definitely hire you.

They don't even interview hard.

head: Drift has|machinery.
body:
1. No direction
2. Fear
3. Distraction
4. Bad environment
5. Weak standards

If nothing is non-negotiable, *everything is optional*. And once everything is optional, drift doesn't have to fight you. It just waits.

The ugliest part isn't that drift delays greatness.

It's that it *retrains a man* to tolerate mediocrity without flinching.

He adjusts downward. He stops expecting sharpness. Stops expecting his own word to mean something in practice.

head: What has drift|already *cost* you|in the last|three years?
body:
Money. Strength. Opportunities. Confidence. Peace. Clarity. Trust. Time.

Write the bill. In writing — not in your head.

Then set one non-negotiable standard. Not ten. One real one.
